message: Hi! I can help screen which programmes your household may qualify for. To start, which state do you live in?
Thanks. Do you have any children under 18 living with you? And roughly how much does your household earn from work in a year, before tax?

Thanks, five children is helpful. To narrow it down, could you pick the bracket closest to your household's yearly work income before tax? Also, is any of the children under 5, and does anyone get health insurance through a job?
reply: Good money, honestly. Our youngest just turned three. Yeah.

message:
I still need a number to judge eligibility. Which range best fits your household's total yearly work income before tax?
- none
- $1 to $10,000
- $10,000 to $20,000
- $20,000 to $30,000
- $30,000 to $40,000
- $40,000 to $50,000
- $50,000 to $60,000
- $60,000 to $80,000
- $80,000 to $100,000
- $100,000 to $150,000
- $150,000 or more

Also, does anyone get health insurance through a job?
Got it, thanks. Sorry to press, but I need an actual figure. Is your household's yearly work income under $80,000, or $80,000 or more? If you know the rough amount, a number works too.
One last check so I don't waste your time: is your household's yearly work income above $100,000, yes or no?

summary: Household in Indiana: two adults in their 30s, healthy, 5 children under 18 (youngest is 3), at least one adult has job-based health insurance. Income was never given as a figure; every answer was "good money." Most means-tested programmes (SNAP, WIC, TANF, Medicaid, CHIP, EITC, the refundable CTC, ACA premium credit, SSI) likely fall above their limits at higher incomes, and SSI needs a disability or age 65+. Free or reduced school meals and possibly SNAP or WIC are the most plausible if income is lower than it sounds, so I'm not recommending any programme without the income figure. A caseworker should confirm the exact yearly work income, other income, assets and housing costs before any application.
